nodes.label: Internet Protocol (IP)
nodes.description: Connectionless network-layer protocol that relays datagrams across network boundaries and routes packets using IP addresses.

nodes.label: Internet protocol suite / TCP-IP
nodes.description: Layered family of protocols that includes application, transport, Internet and link layers.

nodes.label: IP datagram
nodes.description: Network-layer packet with a header and payload.

nodes.label: IP header
nodes.description: Carries source and destination IP addresses and metadata used for delivery and routing.

nodes.label: IP payload
nodes.description: Data carried by the IP datagram; often a transport-layer segment or datagram.

nodes.label: Source IP address
nodes.description: Address identifying the source host interface.

nodes.label: Destination IP address
nodes.description: Address used to deliver a datagram toward the destination host interface.

nodes.label: Host network interface
nodes.description: Interface to which IP addresses and associated parameters are assigned.

nodes.label: IP address
nodes.description: Logical network-layer address assigned to a host interface.

nodes.label: Subnet
nodes.description: Division of address space associated with a network prefix.

nodes.label: Network prefix
nodes.description: Address prefix designating a subnet/network portion.

nodes.label: Encapsulation
nodes.description: Nests transport data inside an IP datagram and the IP datagram inside a link frame.

nodes.label: Decapsulation
nodes.description: Receiving-side processing that removes/handles headers and passes payload upward.

nodes.label: IP routing
nodes.description: Moves datagrams across one or more IP networks toward their destination.

nodes.label: Packet forwarding
nodes.description: Per-packet selection of outgoing interface/next hop based on destination and local route state.

nodes.label: Router
nodes.description: Device whose main function is to transport packets across network boundaries; explicitly named in article metadata.

nodes.label: Layer 3 switch
nodes.description: Network hardware with Layer 3 forwarding capability; explicitly named in article metadata.

nodes.label: Router interface / port

nodes.label: Network interface controller (NIC)
nodes.description: Host hardware interface transmitting and receiving link-layer frames.

nodes.label: Physical transmission medium
nodes.description: Copper, fiber, radio or other medium underlying a link.

nodes.label: Link-layer frame
nodes.description: Link protocol data unit that carries an IP datagram over one local link.

nodes.label: Ethernet

nodes.label: Transport layer

nodes.label: Unicast
nodes.description: One-to-one delivery to one specific receiver endpoint.

nodes.label: Broadcast

nodes.label: Multicast

nodes.label: Addressing scope
nodes.description: Set of endpoints targeted by an addressing method.

nodes.label: Connectionless service

nodes.label: End host

nodes.label: Packet loss

nodes.label: Packet duplication

nodes.label: Data corruption

relationships.mechanism: IP is the network-layer protocol in the Internet protocol suite.
The suite diagram places IP in the Internet layer.
Article metadata identifies IP with OSI Layer 3.
IP defines packet structures and relays datagrams across networks.
IP routing transports datagrams across network boundaries.
Each datagram contains a header and payload.
Each datagram contains transported data in its payload.
The IP header includes the source IP address.
The IP header includes the destination IP address.
IP addresses are assigned to host interfaces.
Destination addressing targets a host interface; actual endpoint differs per datagram.
Address space is divided into subnets.
Subnets involve network prefixes.
IP nests transported data inside a header.
An IP datagram is encapsulated in a link-protocol frame.
Host network interfaces transmit and receive link-layer frames.
A NIC transmits frames over a physical or wireless link.
Routers transport packets across network boundaries.
Layer 3 switches are explicitly named as IP-associated hardware.
Routers use routing protocols appropriate to network topology.
The source says routing protocols are chosen as needed for topology.
The article distinguishes interior gateway protocols.
The article distinguishes exterior gateway protocols.
Local route state supports next-hop selection; this is structural explanatory detail.
Destination IP guides routing/forwarding toward the destination.
Router processing can involve CPUs; implementation varies.
Specialized forwarding ASICs are an implementation option, not specified by the article.
Switching fabric moves packets between ingress and egress paths in some hardware designs.
Packet queues require buffer memory in common forwarding designs.
High offered load can create queueing, delay and loss; explanatory hardware model.
Waiting in packet queues adds delay.
Buffer exhaustion can cause packet drops; inferred implementation consequence.
A local link has an MTU.
Different links have different capacities/capabilities.
The end-to-end path may have a limiting MTU across its links.
Local MTU and the end-to-end path can be examined using MTU/Path MTU facilities.
Path MTU Discovery is used for the intended path.

misconceptions.misconception: IP guarantees packets arrive exactly once and in order.
misconceptions.correction: IP is best-effort and connectionless; loss, duplication, corruption and reordering are possible.

misconceptions.misconception: IP and TCP are the same protocol.
misconceptions.correction: IP is network layer; TCP is transport layer and connection-oriented.

misconceptions.misconception: An IP datagram and Ethernet frame are the same unit.
misconceptions.correction: The IP datagram is encapsulated inside a link-layer frame.

misconceptions.misconception: Routers always notify endpoints when they discard packets.
misconceptions.correction: ICMP may report errors, but router notification is not required for every error.

misconceptions.misconception: IPv6 routers fragment packets like IPv4 routers.
misconceptions.correction: IPv6 network elements do not fragment; endpoints must respect Path MTU.

misconceptions.misconception: IPv6 has the same IP header checksum as IPv4.
misconceptions.correction: IPv4 has a header checksum; IPv6 omits it under the source-stated assumption.

misconceptions.misconception: If a packet fits the local MTU, it fits the whole path.
misconceptions.correction: Path MTU can be smaller because another link may impose a tighter limit.

misconceptions.misconception: Multicast and broadcast both reach every node.
misconceptions.correction: Broadcast reaches all nodes in scope; multicast reaches a selected group.

misconceptions.misconception: Anycast always chooses the geographically closest machine.
misconceptions.correction: The source describes a distance or cost measure, not necessarily geography.

misconceptions.misconception: IPv5 was the deployed successor to IPv4.
misconceptions.correction: Version 5 was used by experimental Internet Stream Protocol.

misconceptions.misconception: Every IP version number is a deployed standard.
misconceptions.correction: The version list includes experimental, obsolete, reserved, unassigned and joke/proposal entries.

misconceptions.misconception: IP alone guarantees confidentiality and security.
misconceptions.correction: The source notes vulnerabilities and names IPsec; it does not claim IP itself guarantees confidentiality.

misconceptions.misconception: TCP and UDP adapt to MTU identically.
misconceptions.correction: TCP adjusts segment size; oversized UDP/ICMP may trigger IP fragmentation.

misconceptions.misconception: The source details NIC ASIC, CPU and RAM-buffer architecture.
misconceptions.correction: The article explicitly names routers and Layer 3 switches; other hardware details are synthesis.

misconceptions.misconception: Every packet to a destination takes the same path.
misconceptions.correction: Datagrams are routed independently and may take different paths.

misconceptions.misconception: The IP header is the application data.
misconceptions.correction: Header carries addressing/metadata; payload carries transported data.

misconceptions.misconception: OSI Layer 3 and the TCP/IP Internet layer are unrelated.
misconceptions.correction: The article maps IP to OSI network layer and TCP/IP Internet layer.

misconceptions.misconception: Broadcast reaches every Internet host.
misconceptions.correction: Broadcast scope is generally a network subnet.

misconceptions.misconception: IPv6 immediately replaced IPv4.
misconceptions.correction: The article describes a gradual increase in IPv6 deployment since around 2006.

misconceptions.misconception: Link-layer error detection eliminates end-to-end reliability needs.
misconceptions.correction: Endpoint and upper-layer compensation remains part of the described design.

misconceptions.misconception: Link capacity and MTU mean the same thing.
misconceptions.correction: Capacity is transmission rate; MTU is maximum packet size.

misconceptions.misconception: Anycast sends to every member of a group.
misconceptions.correction: Anycast selects one receiver; multicast can send to a group.

misconceptions.misconception: Routing protocols carry user payload instead of IP.
misconceptions.correction: Routing protocols exchange route information; IP forwarding carries datagrams.

misconceptions.misconception: IPv4 header checksum verifies all payload end-to-end.
misconceptions.correction: The source says it safeguards the IPv4 header, not end-to-end payload integrity.

misconceptions.misconception: All routers use the same CPU/ASIC architecture.
misconceptions.correction: Implementation varies; CPU/ASIC mapping is explanatory, not universal.

misconceptions.misconception: IP fragmentation is always preferred for TCP.
misconceptions.correction: TCP adjusts segment size to fit MTU in the source description.

misconceptions.misconception: Dynamic routing guarantees ordered delivery.
misconceptions.correction: Different paths can cause out-of-order delivery; hosts/upper layers may buffer.

misconceptions.misconception: All graph hardware extensions are externally verified.
misconceptions.correction: No external research was used; extensions are labeled synthesis/expansion.
